THE LYNCH LAW EXECUTERS IN CALIFORNIA
THE VIGILANCE COMMITTEE'S REACTION.

It will be remembered that when first the intelligence reached us that so-called Vigilance Committee had been formed at San Francisco on Lynch-law principles, and that, instead of endeavoring to make the courts purer and more efficient the committee assumed to be independent of and superior to the law and its officers; we deprecated the whole movement as containing the very essence of anarchy and misrule, as in fact substituting violence and an irresponsible authority for recognised institutions with officers able to rule the people. We saw in that step the introduction of a principle that sooner or later must work mischief for principles indefeasible and operative, and must produce results. The emergency of the case was pressed defy and told that in no other way could life and property be protected; that the committee were also honourable and that the popular sentiment was entirely with them, a fact which undoubtedly at one time was true, shown by the hideous longing for an exception evinced by the populace when Whitaker and McKenzie hung.

The ground assumed in these columns with reference to the vigilance committee system was, that it was wrong in principle and therefore eventually become wrong in practice; that assumption of authority vested elsewhere by the people, and by them legally transferred to the vigilance committee, was not merely a local pattern of magisterial and executive power but violent opposition to the laws and constitution of the State; that its despotic administration of life and death, of unheard-of punishments, and of Chamber examinations and convictions, all tending to demoralize and debase the people, by making them familiar with summary convictions and executions without the show of mercy or semblance of decent ceremony. The last narrative that published of these executions, truly horrifying, and thus justified our censures and prophecies, is here upon us, as described by an independent writer and citizen of San Francisco:

"Two of the vigilance committee have alienated from them some of their best friends as well as a large majority of this community. You have already heard of the execution by this committee of Whitaker and McKenzie on Sunday. Suffice to say that that horrid deed has so shocked this community that confidence in the humanity and prudence of the committee has been again to be restored. This community contends if they were so wanting in vigilance to permit the authorities to take the prisoners from them, they should have let them pass and determined to be careful in future; but this breaking into the prison, and in spirit of retaliation upon the authorities, hanging these guilty men on Sunday is an outrage which the better part of the community cannot make either to sanction or tolerate. This committee will hereafter only be commended for any lawful efforts which they may use in bringing criminals to justice, but the time is past when this community will permit them to become Judges and executioners."

Another move which has already rendered the committee unpopular, is the effort on the part of many of its leading members to get up what have called land monopoly schemes at the elections. This has caused some to believe that the extensive land claimants and wealthy will, in some way or other, use this vigilance committee to favor their own selfish ends. We do not know whether these fears are groundless or otherwise, but the truth is the committee has the bone and sinew of this community with it, and is safe to infer that its authority will again be executed.

That the vigilance committee is losing the confidence of leading men, and becoming the subject of suspicion and surmising, is not to be wondered at. The only marvel is that such despotic and dangerous power has been permitted to establish itself upon its present basis. But what will follow this reaction of public sentiment? Will the members of the committee themselves be safe from reprisals? May the same people who delighted when the committee stole prisoners from the city Jail and gave an exhibition of double execution the Sabbath, may this populace have its second thought and join the authorities in demanding from the committee the evidence of its legal right to condemn and hang for crimes which the constitution does not punish with death? And how the committee prepared for such a day of reckoning is one thing; to suspend from a beam and jerk him up and down until he is killed as in the above Sunday execution, amid the howlings of the crowd, is another and widely different thing.

The moral tribunal which, by the silent but unceasing operation of a great principle, has recovered its authority with the people, can now punish those who assumed its powers and exercised, and even exceeded, its prerogatives.
